chunks: Examples of embedded systems. The question: What are some examples of embedded systems?
The question asks you to name products with a small dedicated computer inside and say what makes each tricky to build.
Examples are everywhere: microwaves, thermostats, TV remotes, car brake controllers, pacemakers, drones and routers.
Each runs one fixed job, reads the world through sensors, and controls something.
The useful way to tell them apart is by their main limit: tight cost, tiny battery, strict timing, or safety.
Picture keeping a bath at the right temperature. You touch the water, decide it is too cold, open the hot tap a bit, and check again.
That repeating cycle of sense, decide, act is what most embedded systems do. The difference is the stakes. In a bath, being a few seconds late doesn't matter.
In an airbag, a few milliseconds late is a failure.
A typical embedded control loop: read the sensor, run the control law, drive the actuator; the physical process closes the loop back to the sensor.
Sensor: a part that measures something real, such as temperature or wheel speed. Actuator: a part that does something physical, such as a motor, heater, valve or lamp.
Control loop: the repeating cycle of reading sensors, deciding, and driving actuators. Real-time: the answer has to arrive by a deadline to count as correct.
Hard real-time: missing a deadline is a failure, not just a slowdown. Constraint: a limit on cost, battery life, size or timing.
A thermostat reads a temperature sensor, turns the heater on at 20 degrees Celsius and off at 21 degrees Celsius, and repeats. Nothing is urgent, so a cheap chip is enough.
Now take a car engine at 6000 rpm (turns per minute).
That is 100 turns per second, so one turn takes 10 milliseconds (thousandths of a second), and one degree of rotation lasts 10 milliseconds over 360 about 28 microseconds (millionths of a second).
The spark must be timed to about that precision, so dedicated timer circuits on the chip handle it. Same loop, very different constraints. That is the whole idea.

"An embedded system is a computer dedicated to one job inside a product: a microwave, a thermostat, a TV remote, a car's engine and ABS controllers, a pacemaker, a drone's flight controller, a router, a 3D printer.
They differ by what constrains them: pacemakers are ultra-low power and safety-critical, ABS and engine control are hard real-time, remotes are cost-driven, routers are throughput-driven.
For example, an engine controller must time ignition to within a fraction of a crank degree, about 28 microseconds at 6000 rpm."
